specStatements.text: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures. Melting point and boiling point data can be used to distinguish pure substances from mixtures.
In everyday language, a pure substance can mean a substance that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk.
Students should be able to use melting point and boiling point data to distinguish pure from impure substances.

A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product. Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose. Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties. Formulations include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods.
Students should be able to identify formulations given appropriate information.
Students do not need to know the names of components in proprietary products.

Chromatography can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances. Chromatography involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase. Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases.
The ratio of the distance moved by a compound (centre of spot from origin) to the distance moved by the solvent can be expressed as its Rf value:
R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent)

Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, which can be used to help identify the compounds. The compounds in a mixture may separate into different spots depending on the solvent but a pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents.
explain how paper chromatography separates mixtures
suggest how chromatographic methods can be used for distinguishing pure substances from impure substances
interpret chromatograms and determine Rf values from chromatograms
provide answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
Required practical 6: investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances. Students should calculate Rf values.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of components in proprietary products.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Formulations are taught only through the categories the specification itself lists - fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods - and through the general idea that each component is present in a measured quantity for a particular purpose. Where a product appears in a question, its components are described by their job (pigment, binder, solvent; active ingredient, filler, coating) or given as an unnamed percentage list, never as the trade formula of a named brand. No question requires recall of what is in any commercial paint, detergent, medicine, fertiliser or food product, and no such ingredient list is presented as material to learn. Students are asked only to decide whether the information given describes a formulation.

concepts.definition: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. Purity is about what the sample contains, not about where it came from or how clean it looks.
Two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined. A mixture is not a pure substance, however carefully it has been made and however uniform it looks.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes between solid and liquid. A pure substance melts at one temperature, and that value can be compared with accepted data.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes between liquid and gas. A pure substance boils at one temperature under fixed conditions.

concepts.term: Melting or boiling over a range
concepts.definition: A mixture does not melt or boil at one specific temperature; the change happens over a range of temperatures. A measured range, rather than a single sharp value, is the evidence that a sample is a mixture and not a pure substance.

In everyday language, a pure substance can mean a substance that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk. Such a product is usually a mixture in the chemical sense.
A mixture that has been designed as a useful product. Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose.
Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties. Changing the quantities changes how the product behaves.
Formulations include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. They can be solid, liquid or gaseous products.
A separation method that can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances.
The phase in a chromatography experiment that does not move. In paper chromatography the stationary phase is the paper.
The phase that moves through the stationary phase, carrying substances with it. In paper chromatography the mobile phase is the solvent moving up the paper.

Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases. A substance that spends more of its time in the mobile phase is carried further up the paper; one held more strongly by the stationary phase moves less far.
The finished paper, showing the pencil origin line, the marked solvent front and the separated spots. It is interpreted by counting spots and by measuring distances to calculate Rf values.
The pencil line on which the spots are placed at the start. All distances moved by a substance are measured from this line to the centre of its spot.
The furthest point reached by the solvent, marked as soon as the paper is taken out. The distance moved by the solvent is measured from the origin to this line.

The ratio of the distance moved by a compound (centre of spot from origin) to the distance moved by the solvent. It is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no units, and because a substance cannot travel further than the solvent that carries it, its value lies between 0 and 1.
Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent. Both distances are measured in the same unit, from the origin line.

The compounds in a mixture may separate into different spots depending on the solvent, but a pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents. One spot in one solvent alone is therefore not proof of purity.

Investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances, calculating Rf values. The origin line is drawn in pencil, the solvent starts below that line, the paper is removed before the solvent reaches the top and the solvent front is marked at once.

An Rf value is quoted to no more significant figures than the measurements it came from. Distances read to the nearest millimetre give two significant figures, so an Rf value is normally given to two significant figures rather than to all the digits on the calculator.

misconceptions.question: A carton says 'pure orange juice'. Is the juice pure in the chemical sense?
misconceptions.correct: No. Nothing has been added to it, which is the everyday meaning of pure, but chemically it is a mixture of water, sugars, acids and many other compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: If a label says pure, then the substance must be a pure chemical, because pure means the same thing in science as it does on packaging.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification's own point is that the two meanings differ. Advertising uses pure to mean unadulterated and natural, and students meet that use thousands of times before they meet the chemical definition once.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what is in the sample, not what has been done to it. Chemically pure means a single element or compound and nothing else. Orange juice contains many compounds, so it is a mixture no matter what the carton says.

misconceptions.question: Can a compound such as water be a pure substance?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A pure substance is a single element or compound, so a sample containing only water is pure.
misconceptions.misconception: A compound contains more than one element, so it is already a sort of mixture and cannot count as pure. Only elements can be really pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear 'more than one kind of atom' and map it onto 'more than one substance'. The word mixture and the idea of being made of different elements get run together.
misconceptions.correction: The elements in a compound are chemically combined into one new substance with its own fixed properties. Water is one compound, so a sample of nothing but water is pure. Purity counts substances, not elements.

misconceptions.question: A colourless, clear liquid with nothing floating in it - is it pure?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Sea water and dilute salt solution both look clear and colourless, and both are mixtures.
misconceptions.misconception: If a sample looks clean and clear, with no cloudiness or bits in it, then it is pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday judgements of purity are visual, and filtration in earlier science removes visible solids and leaves a clear liquid, which students read as a purification that has finished the job.
misconceptions.correction: Dissolved substances are invisible. Judge purity by evidence about composition, such as a sharp melting or boiling point or a single chromatography spot, not by appearance.

misconceptions.question: Does a mixture melt at one specific temperature?
misconceptions.correct: No. Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures; a mixture melts or boils over a range of temperatures.
misconceptions.misconception: Every substance melts at its own single temperature, so the sharpness of the change tells you nothing; you can only compare the number with a data book.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Data tables list one melting point for everything students meet, so the idea that a change of state can be spread over several degrees never appears until purity is taught.
misconceptions.correction: Watch the thermometer, not just the final value. A pure substance stays at one temperature while it melts; a mixture melts gradually across a range. The range itself is the evidence of a mixture.

misconceptions.question: A solid melts between 78 and 82 degrees C, and the data book value is 80 degrees C. Is it pure?
misconceptions.correct: No. Melting spread over a four degree range shows a mixture, even though the range happens to straddle the accepted value.
misconceptions.misconception: As long as the temperature is close to the book value, the sample is pure; a few degrees either side is just experimental error.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are trained to allow for measurement uncertainty, and they apply that habit to a range that is actually chemical evidence rather than instrument error.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish uncertainty in one reading from a genuine range of melting. A pure solid gives one temperature, read with its own small uncertainty. A sample that keeps melting as the temperature climbs is impure.

misconceptions.question: Is muddy river water a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a mixture, but it has not been designed as a useful product with components in measured quantities.
misconceptions.misconception: A formulation is just another word for a mixture, so anything with more than one substance in it is a formulation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition begins with the word mixture, and students stop reading there. The design and measurement half of the definition is treated as description rather than as part of the test.
misconceptions.correction: Apply both halves of the definition. A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product, with each chemical present in a measured quantity for a particular purpose. River water fails on design, purpose and measurement.

misconceptions.question: Must a formulation be a liquid?
misconceptions.correct: No. Formulations include alloys, fertilisers and foods, which are solids, as well as fuels, paints and cleaning agents.
misconceptions.misconception: Formulations are liquids you mix up, like paints, medicines and cleaning products, so solids are not formulations.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The examples students meet first are usually liquids, and the word formulation sounds like formula, recipe and solution, all of which suggest something poured and stirred.
misconceptions.correction: State of matter is irrelevant. What matters is that the product is a designed mixture with measured components. Brass, a fertiliser blend and a loaf of bread all qualify.

misconceptions.question: Is an alloy such as brass a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The specification lists alloys among formulations; the metals are mixed in measured quantities to give the required properties.
misconceptions.misconception: Formulations are things made by chemists in the pharmaceutical or paint industry, so medicines and paints count but alloys and foods do not.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word formulation is met most often in the context of medicines, and metals are studied in a separate topic, so students file alloys under bonding rather than under mixtures.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the specification's own list: fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. Any designed mixture with measured components counts, whatever industry makes it.

misconceptions.question: A product is made by mixing three chemicals in fixed proportions. Is it a compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fixed proportions in a recipe are not chemical combination; the product is still a mixture, and a formulation.
misconceptions.misconception: If the amounts are fixed and measured, the substances must be chemically combined, so the product is a compound with a formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fixed ratios are used earlier as the hallmark of a compound. Students carry that rule across without noticing that in a compound the ratio is fixed by the bonding, not chosen by a manufacturer.
misconceptions.correction: In a compound the ratio is fixed by chemistry and cannot be changed. In a formulation the ratio is chosen by the designer and could be changed, which would change the product's properties. The components stay chemically separate.

misconceptions.question: In paper chromatography, which is the stationary phase?
misconceptions.correct: The paper is the stationary phase; the solvent moving through it is the mobile phase.
misconceptions.misconception: The solvent sits still in the beaker so it must be the stationary phase, and the paper does the work of separating so it must be the mobile phase.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look at the apparatus at the start, when the solvent is a still pool and the paper is the object being handled, rather than at what moves during the run.
misconceptions.correction: Name the phases by what happens during the separation. The solvent travels up the paper, so it is mobile. The paper never moves, so it is stationary.

misconceptions.question: Does the lightest substance in a mixture always travel furthest up the paper?
misconceptions.correct: No. How far a substance travels depends on its distribution between the two phases, not on the mass of its particles.
misconceptions.misconception: Chromatography works like a race in which small, light particles are carried up easily and heavy ones are left behind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Separation techniques met earlier, such as filtration and settling, do sort by particle size or density, and gravity offers an intuitive story that fits.
misconceptions.correction: The solvent does not lift particles by weight. A substance moves far because it spends more time dissolved in the mobile phase and less held by the paper.

misconceptions.question: A substance is strongly attracted to the paper. Does it travel a long way?
misconceptions.correct: No. Being held strongly by the stationary phase keeps a substance near the origin, giving a low Rf value.
misconceptions.misconception: The substance that sticks to the paper best must be the one the paper carries furthest, so strong attraction to the paper means a high spot.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word attracted is read as helpful rather than as holding back, and students do not picture the paper as a brake acting against the moving solvent.
misconceptions.correction: Set the two attractions against each other. Attraction to the paper holds a substance back; attraction to the solvent carries it forward. High Rf means the solvent wins.

misconceptions.question: A spot moved 3.0 cm and the solvent moved 6.0 cm. Is the Rf value 2.0?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent, so the Rf value is 0.50.
misconceptions.misconception: Rf is the distance moved by the solvent divided by the distance moved by the substance, because you divide the big number by the small one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that a division is needed but not its direction, and the habit of dividing larger by smaller to avoid decimals decides it for them.
misconceptions.correction: Write the equation out before substituting: substance on top, solvent underneath. Because the solvent always travels at least as far as the substance, a correct Rf value can never be greater than 1.

misconceptions.question: Where are the two distances measured from?
misconceptions.correct: Both are measured from the origin, the pencil line: to the centre of the spot, and to the solvent front.
misconceptions.misconception: You measure from the bottom edge of the paper, or up to the top of the paper, because those are the ends of the strip.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The paper's edges are the obvious landmarks and are easy to line a ruler against, while the pencil line looks like a place to put spots rather than a measuring datum.
misconceptions.correction: The origin is the starting line for everything. The paper below it and above the solvent front took no part in the separation, so neither edge is measured from or to.

misconceptions.question: Which part of a spot is measured to?
misconceptions.correct: The centre of the spot, as the specification states.
misconceptions.misconception: Measure to the top edge of the spot, since that is as far as the substance actually reached.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Spots spread as they travel, so students look for a single definite boundary, and the leading edge feels like the honest limit of the substance's journey.
misconceptions.correction: Use the centre every time. A spot spreads in both directions, so its centre represents the substance's position; using an edge inflates or deflates every Rf value.

misconceptions.question: What unit does an Rf value have?
misconceptions.correct: None. Rf is a ratio of two distances measured in the same unit, so the units cancel.
misconceptions.misconception: Rf comes from measuring lengths in centimetres, so the answer must be in centimetres too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are correctly drilled to attach units to every measured quantity, and they apply the rule to a derived quantity without checking what happens to the units in the division.
misconceptions.correction: Divide the units as well as the numbers: cm divided by cm leaves nothing. Quote Rf as a bare number such as 0.45.

misconceptions.question: Can a substance have an Rf value of 1.4?
misconceptions.correct: No. The substance is carried by the solvent, so it cannot pass the solvent front; Rf lies between 0 and 1.
misconceptions.misconception: In a really good solvent a substance can be pushed past the solvent front, so Rf values above 1 are possible.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rf is treated as an abstract number from a formula rather than as a fraction of a journey, so nothing warns the student that a value above 1 is physically impossible.
misconceptions.correction: Use the range as a check on your arithmetic. If a calculation gives a number above 1, the two distances have been divided the wrong way round.

misconceptions.question: Is a compound's Rf value the same in every solvent?
misconceptions.correct: No. Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, and this is what makes chromatography useful for identification.
misconceptions.misconception: Rf is a fixed property of a compound, like its melting point, so one measured value can be looked up in any table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rf is introduced alongside melting point as a way of identifying substances, so students assume it behaves like a constant of the substance alone.
misconceptions.correction: Rf describes how a compound is distributed between one particular pair of phases. Change the solvent and the distribution changes, so the value changes. Comparisons are only valid within the same solvent and conditions.

misconceptions.question: A sample gives one spot in one solvent. Is it pure?
misconceptions.correct: Not proved. A pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents, so one solvent alone is not enough.
misconceptions.misconception: One spot means one substance, so a single run showing a single spot proves the sample is pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'one spot equals one substance' is a fair summary of what is seen and is easy to remember, and students rarely meet a case where two compounds happen not to separate.
misconceptions.correction: Two compounds can have the same Rf value in one solvent and travel together as one spot. Repeat the chromatography in a different solvent; only a substance that still gives one spot is evidence of purity.

misconceptions.question: An unknown spot has the same Rf value as a known dye. Are they the same compound?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Matching Rf values in one solvent is evidence that helps identify a compound, not proof.
misconceptions.misconception: Rf values are like fingerprints, so an exact match identifies the substance beyond doubt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'used to identify' is read as 'proves the identity of', and students are used to tests that give a definite yes or no answer.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says chromatography gives information to help identify substances. Strengthen the evidence by running the unknown and the known side by side in more than one solvent.

misconceptions.question: Can a chromatogram alone tell you the names of the substances in a mixture?
misconceptions.correct: No. It separates the mixture and gives information to help identify substances, usually by comparison with known reference substances.
misconceptions.misconception: The chromatogram itself names the substances, because each substance has its own place on the paper.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook chromatograms are drawn with the known substances already labelled, so the labels look as though they came from the paper rather than from separate reference runs.
misconceptions.correction: A spot is a position, not a name. Run known substances on the same paper in the same solvent and compare, or compare Rf values obtained under the same conditions.

misconceptions.question: Can the origin line be drawn in pen?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is drawn in pencil, because ink would dissolve in the solvent and travel up the paper.
misconceptions.misconception: A pen is fine as long as the ink is a different colour from the substances being tested, so the lines cannot be confused.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the concern is about confusing the results and think the problem is only one of telling colours apart, rather than of the line itself moving.
misconceptions.correction: Ink is itself a mixture of soluble dyes, so it separates and runs, destroying the origin line the measurements depend on. Pencil is insoluble in the solvent and stays where it was drawn.

misconceptions.question: Should the solvent cover the spots at the start?
misconceptions.correct: No. The solvent level must be below the origin line so the spots are not washed off the paper.
misconceptions.misconception: The spots have to be under the solvent so that they can dissolve and start moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dissolving is understood as something that needs immersion, so leaving the spots above the liquid looks as though nothing will happen to them.
misconceptions.correction: The solvent rises through the paper by itself and reaches the spots from below. If the spots start below the surface they dissolve straight into the pool of solvent and are lost from the paper.

misconceptions.question: Distances of 34 mm and 75 mm give 0.453333 on the calculator. What should be written down?
misconceptions.correct: 0.45, because the measurements were made to two significant figures.
misconceptions.misconception: Copying more digits from the calculator makes the answer more accurate, so the full display should be written down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Precision and accuracy are confused: extra digits look like extra care, and there is nothing on the calculator to say where the reliable digits stop.
misconceptions.correction: An answer cannot be more precise than the measurements behind it. Distances read to the nearest millimetre give two significant figures, so the Rf value is quoted to two significant figures.

misconceptions.question: Salt is pure and water is pure. Is salt solution pure?
misconceptions.correct: No. It contains two compounds, so it is a mixture even though each component on its own is pure.
misconceptions.misconception: If every substance you put in was pure, then what you get out must be pure as well, because nothing dirty was added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Purity is understood as the absence of contamination, so adding something deliberately and cleanly does not feel like making the sample impure.
misconceptions.correction: Purity is about how many substances are present, not how clean they were. One element or compound only is pure; two, however carefully combined, make a mixture.

misconceptions.question: Is a natural spring water purer than a compound made in a factory?
misconceptions.correct: Not chemically. Spring water is a mixture of water and dissolved minerals; a laboratory sample containing one compound only is pure.
misconceptions.misconception: Natural and untouched means pure, while anything manufactured or processed has been contaminated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of pure carries the idea of being in its natural state, and marketing reinforces the link between natural and pure.
misconceptions.correction: Origin does not decide purity. Ask only whether the sample is a single element or compound. Many manufactured substances are pure and many natural ones are mixtures.

misconceptions.question: A solid softens from 70 degrees C and is fully liquid at 80 degrees C. Is it pure?
misconceptions.correct: No. It changed state over a ten degree range, so it is a mixture, whatever the final temperature was.
misconceptions.misconception: The melting point is the temperature at which melting finishes, so if that final value matches the data book the sample is pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students watch for the moment the last solid disappears because that is the clearest event to record, and they treat the gradual softening beforehand as warming up.
misconceptions.correction: Record the whole range, from the first sign of melting to the last. A pure substance melts entirely at one temperature; a range of any size is evidence of a mixture.

misconceptions.question: A liquid's temperature rises from 97 to 103 degrees C while it boils. Is that just the heating rate?
misconceptions.correct: No. A rising temperature during boiling shows the liquid is a mixture.
misconceptions.misconception: Any range in a change of state is caused by the equipment - heating too fast, a slow thermometer or uneven warming - rather than by the substance itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught to blame apparatus for unexpected results, and a Bunsen burner really does heat unevenly, so the explanation feels well trained rather than evasive.
misconceptions.correction: A pure liquid stays at its boiling point however hard it is heated, because the extra energy goes into the change of state. A temperature that climbs while the liquid boils means more than one substance is present.

misconceptions.question: Copper wire is manufactured and useful. Is it a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Copper is a pure element, and a formulation must be a mixture.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything made deliberately for a job is a formulation, because it was designed as a useful product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The memorable part of the definition is 'designed as a useful product', and the requirement that it be a mixture is skipped over as an obvious preliminary.
misconceptions.correction: Check for a mixture first. A single element or compound, however useful and however carefully manufactured, cannot be a formulation. Brass is a formulation; pure copper is not.

misconceptions.question: Are the spots the mobile phase?
misconceptions.correct: No. The mobile phase is the solvent; the spots are the substances being separated, carried by it.
misconceptions.misconception: The mobile phase must be whatever moves up the paper, and what you watch moving is the coloured spots.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The colours are the only visible thing that moves, and the solvent front is easy to overlook, so students name the phase after what they can see.
misconceptions.correction: The phases are the two things the substances are shared between: the paper and the solvent. The substances being analysed are not a phase at all; they distribute themselves between the two.

misconceptions.question: Why does the origin line have to be pencil rather than pen?
misconceptions.correct: Because pencil is insoluble in the solvent, so the line does not move or contaminate the chromatogram.
misconceptions.misconception: Pencil is used because a sharp pencil draws a thinner, neater line, which makes the distances easier to measure accurately.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Precision of measurement is a real concern in this practical, so a reason about accuracy sounds sensible and the student never has to think about solubility.
misconceptions.correction: The issue is chemical, not geometrical. Ink dissolves in the solvent and runs up the paper with the samples; pencil graphite does not dissolve, so the starting line stays put.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter how deep the solvent is, as long as it touches the paper?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It must be below the origin line, otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent instead of travelling up the paper.
misconceptions.misconception: The depth only affects how fast the solvent climbs, so any level that wets the paper will do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think about the solvent's job of moving up the paper and not about what a pool of solvent would do to a spot sitting in it.
misconceptions.correction: Set the level below the pencil line every time. Depth is not about speed; it is about keeping the samples on the paper where they can separate.

misconceptions.question: Does a bigger spot mean there is more of that substance?
misconceptions.correct: That is not what the specification asks chromatography to show. It separates mixtures and gives information to help identify substances.
misconceptions.misconception: The size or darkness of a spot measures how much of the substance the mixture contained, so a chromatogram gives the composition by amount.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bigger looks like more in almost every other context, and spot sizes on a real chromatogram do vary noticeably, so the inference is tempting.
misconceptions.correction: Read a chromatogram for how many substances are present and how far each has travelled. Use the number of spots and their Rf values, not their size, to answer questions about separation and identity.

mcqs.stem: In chemistry, which of these samples counts as a pure substance?

options.text: Spring water sold as natural, with nothing added to it
options.rationale: The everyday meaning of pure, unadulterated and in its natural state, is taken as the chemical meaning.

options.text: Sea water, because water and salt are both pure chemicals
options.rationale: Students judge purity by whether the components were clean rather than by how many there are.

options.text: Clean air, because its gases are clear and dry throughout
options.rationale: A sample that looks clear and uniform is assumed to contain only one substance.

options.text: Distilled water, a single compound with nothing else in it
options.rationale: A pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.

mcqs.stem: A student says a compound cannot be pure because it contains more than one element. What is wrong with this?

options.text: A compound is one substance, so a compound alone is pure
options.rationale: The specification counts a single element or a single compound as pure; the number of elements combined is irrelevant.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since only elements can be classed as pure
options.rationale: 'More than one kind of atom' is read as 'more than one substance', so compounds are excluded.

options.text: A compound is pure only if just two elements are combined
options.rationale: The same confusion, softened into a rule that allows simple compounds but not complex ones.

options.text: A compound is pure only if it was made in a laboratory
options.rationale: Purity is attributed to how the sample was produced rather than to what it contains.

mcqs.stem: Four solid samples were heated gently. Which result shows a pure substance?

options.text: It melted steadily between 65 and 79 degrees C as it warmed
options.rationale: Students who think every substance melts over a range see nothing wrong with this result.

options.text: It melted at 80 degrees C, with no change over a range
options.rationale: Pure elements and compounds melt at specific temperatures, so melting at one fixed value is the evidence of purity.

options.text: It melted between 78 and 82 degrees C, close to the true value
options.rationale: A range straddling the book value is read as experimental uncertainty rather than as a mixture.

options.text: It melted at 80 degrees C after softening from 70 degrees C
options.rationale: The final temperature matches the data book, so the earlier softening is dismissed as warming up.

mcqs.stem: Liquid A boils steadily at 100 degrees C. Liquid B starts boiling at 97 degrees C and the temperature rises to 103 degrees C. What can be concluded?

options.text: A is a pure substance and B is a mixture
options.rationale: A pure liquid boils at a specific temperature; a boiling range shows that B is a mixture.

options.text: Both are pure, but B was heated too quickly
options.rationale: The range is blamed on the apparatus rather than on the composition of the liquid.

options.text: B is pure, since it boiled near 100 degrees C
options.rationale: The student anchors on the familiar value of 100 and ignores the range.

options.text: A is a mixture, as it boiled at one temperature
options.rationale: The rule is inverted, with a single fixed temperature taken as the sign of a mixture.

mcqs.stem: A carton is labelled 'pure milk'. What does the label mean?

options.text: Nothing has been added; chemically the milk is a mixture
options.rationale: This is the everyday meaning given in the specification: unadulterated and in its natural state, though chemically milk is a mixture.

options.text: The milk is a single compound, so it is chemically pure
options.rationale: The label's word 'pure' is read as the chemical definition.

options.text: The milk is pure because it is white with nothing in it
options.rationale: Purity is judged from the uniform appearance of the liquid.

options.text: The milk is pure because each substance in it is pure
options.rationale: A mixture of clean components is assumed to be pure itself.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the definition of a formulation?

options.text: Any mixture of two or more substances, however it was made
options.rationale: Only the first word of the definition is used, and the design and measurement are dropped.

options.text: A liquid in which several solids have been fully dissolved
options.rationale: Formulations are assumed to be liquid products because the familiar examples are.

options.text: A pure compound made by reacting measured amounts together
options.rationale: Measured quantities are taken to imply chemical combination into a compound.

options.text: A mixture designed as a useful product, in measured quantities
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: a mixture designed as a useful product, mixed in carefully measured quantities.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a formulation?

options.text: Muddy river water, a mixture of soil, water and dissolved salts
options.rationale: It is a mixture, and formulation is treated as another word for mixture.

options.text: Paint, mixed from pigment, binder and solvent in set amounts
options.rationale: Paint is named in the specification's list and is a mixture whose components are measured to give the required properties.

options.text: Copper, a pure metal drawn into wire for electrical wiring
options.rationale: A useful manufactured product is assumed to be a formulation even though it is one element.

options.text: Sodium chloride, a compound added to food in measured amounts
options.rationale: The measured amount is mistaken for the defining feature, though the substance is a single compound.

mcqs.stem: A product label lists five ingredients, each with a percentage and a stated job such as cleaning, thickening or perfuming. What does this show?

options.text: It is a pure substance, since every ingredient is listed
options.rationale: A full ingredients list is read as a guarantee that nothing unwanted is present, and so as purity.

options.text: It is a formulation, as each measured part has a purpose
options.rationale: Components in measured quantities, each with a particular purpose, is exactly what identifies a formulation.

options.text: It is a compound, because the parts are in fixed amounts
options.rationale: Fixed proportions are the rule students learned for compounds, and it is applied here.

options.text: It is a formulation only if the product is a medicine
options.rationale: Formulations are thought to belong only to the pharmaceutical industry.

mcqs.stem: Why is brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, described as a formulation?

options.text: It is not one, because formulations must be liquid products
options.rationale: Solids are excluded because the examples students recall are liquids.

options.text: Its metals combine chemically in a fixed ratio when melted
options.rationale: A measured ratio is taken to mean the metals have formed a compound.

options.text: Its metals are mixed in measured amounts for useful properties
options.rationale: Alloys are in the specification's list of formulations, and the proportions are chosen to give the required properties.

options.text: It is not one, because alloys are only studied as metals
options.rationale: Alloys are filed under bonding rather than under designed mixtures.

mcqs.stem: In paper chromatography, which statement about the phases is correct?

options.text: The solvent is the stationary phase and the paper is mobile
options.rationale: The still pool of solvent at the start is taken as stationary and the paper as the active part.

options.text: The spots are the stationary phase and the paper is mobile
options.rationale: The substances themselves are wrongly treated as one of the phases.

options.text: The paper is the stationary phase and the spots are mobile
options.rationale: Half right: the visible moving colours are named as the mobile phase instead of the solvent.

options.text: The paper is the stationary phase and the solvent is mobile
options.rationale: The paper does not move; the solvent travels through it carrying the substances.

mcqs.stem: Why do the substances in a mixture end up at different heights on a chromatogram?

options.text: The lightest particles are carried furthest up the paper
options.rationale: Separation is imagined as sorting by mass, as in filtration or settling.

options.text: Substances held most strongly by the paper travel furthest
options.rationale: Attraction to the stationary phase is read as help rather than as a brake.

options.text: They are distributed differently between the two phases
options.rationale: The specification states that separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases.

options.text: Each substance travels a distance fixed by its own colour
options.rationale: Because the spots are coloured, colour is assumed to be the property that controls the movement.

mcqs.stem: Which substance in a mixture moves furthest up the paper?

options.text: The one with the smallest and lightest particles in the mixture
options.rationale: The run is pictured as a race won by the lightest particles.

options.text: The one held most strongly by the paper it soaks through
options.rationale: Strong attraction to the paper is mistaken for being carried well by it.

options.text: The one most attracted to the solvent and least to the paper
options.rationale: Spending more time in the mobile phase and less held by the stationary phase carries a substance furthest.

options.text: The one placed on the pencil line in the largest single spot
options.rationale: Spot size is assumed to control the outcome rather than the distribution between phases.

mcqs.stem: Which expression gives the Rf value of a substance?

options.text: distance moved by solvent / distance moved by substance
options.rationale: The division is inverted, usually to avoid producing a decimal answer.

options.text: distance moved by substance / total length of the paper
options.rationale: The edge of the paper is used as the reference instead of the solvent front.

options.text: distance moved by solvent / distance left above the spot
options.rationale: Both the direction of the division and the measured distance are confused.

options.text: distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
options.rationale: This is the equation exactly as the specification states it.

mcqs.stem: When finding how far a substance has moved on a chromatogram, where is the distance measured?

options.text: From the pencil line to the centre of the spot
options.rationale: The specification specifies the centre of the spot measured from the origin.

options.text: From the pencil line to the top edge of the spot
options.rationale: The leading edge is taken as the furthest the substance reached.

options.text: From the bottom of the paper to the spot's centre
options.rationale: The edge of the paper is an easier landmark to line a ruler against than the origin.

options.text: From the base of the spot up to the solvent front
options.rationale: The two distances required by the equation are merged into one measurement.

mcqs.stem: On a chromatogram the centre of a spot is 3.6 cm from the pencil line, and the solvent front is 8.0 cm from the pencil line. What is the Rf value of the substance?

options.rationale: 8.0 / 3.6 divides the larger distance by the smaller one.
3.6 / 8.0 = 0.45, a ratio with no units, given to two significant figures.

options.text: 4.4 cm
options.rationale: The distances are subtracted rather than divided, leaving a length.
The arithmetic is right but a unit is attached to a ratio.

mcqs.stem: A spot moved 34 mm and the solvent moved 75 mm, both measured to the nearest millimetre. How should the Rf value be given?

options.rationale: Digits are copied from the calculator in the belief that more digits mean more accuracy.
Both measurements have two significant figures, so the Rf value is quoted to two significant figures.
Over-rounded to one significant figure, discarding a digit the measurements support.
A unit is attached even though the millimetres cancel in the division.

mcqs.stem: Why can the same compound have a different Rf value in a different solvent?

options.text: It cannot, because each compound has one fixed Rf value
options.rationale: Rf is treated as a constant of the compound, like its melting point.

options.text: Its distribution between the phases changes with the solvent
options.rationale: Rf depends on how the compound is shared between that particular solvent and the paper, so a new solvent gives a new value.

options.text: In a new solvent the paper always holds the compound more
options.rationale: The change is blamed on the paper alone rather than on the balance between the phases.

options.text: The compound moves further than the solvent in some liquids
options.rationale: Rf values above 1 are thought possible in a particularly good solvent.

mcqs.stem: A sample gives one spot when run in a single solvent. What can be concluded?

options.text: It is definitely pure, because only one spot developed
options.rationale: The rule 'one spot means one substance' is applied to a single run.

options.text: It is the same compound as every sample giving one spot
options.rationale: A single spot is treated as an identification rather than as evidence about purity.

options.text: It may be pure; it must give one spot in all solvents
options.rationale: The specification requires a single spot in all solvents before a compound is taken to be pure.

options.text: Nothing follows, because no Rf value has been calculated
options.rationale: The chromatogram is thought to be meaningless until a number is worked out from it.

mcqs.stem: Which chromatography result is evidence that a sample is impure?

options.text: It separated into three spots when one solvent was used
options.rationale: More than one spot shows more than one compound is present, so the sample is a mixture.

options.text: It gave a single spot in each of three different solvents
options.rationale: The strongest evidence of purity is misread as evidence of the opposite.

options.text: Its single spot had the same Rf value as a known dye
options.rationale: A matching Rf value is treated as a finding about contamination rather than about identity.

options.text: Its single spot had a much larger area than the others
options.rationale: Spot size is assumed to carry information about what the sample contains.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 6, why is the line on which the spots are placed drawn in pencil?

options.text: A pen line works too if the ink is a different colour
options.rationale: The problem is thought to be only that the colours might be confused.

options.text: A pencil line can be drawn far more thinly than ink
options.rationale: A reason about measuring accurately sounds sensible and avoids the chemistry.

options.text: Pencil does not dissolve, so the line stays in place
options.rationale: Graphite is insoluble in the solvent, so the origin line does not run and the measurements stay valid.

options.text: Ink would react chemically with the dyes in the spots
options.rationale: Ink is known to be a problem, but the reason given is a reaction rather than dissolving.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 6, why must the solvent in the beaker start below the pencil line?

options.text: Otherwise the solvent cannot dissolve the spots at all
options.rationale: Dissolving is assumed to need immersion, so the reason is inverted.

options.text: Otherwise the solvent would rise up the paper too fast
options.rationale: The depth of solvent is thought to matter only for the speed of the run.

options.text: Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent and are lost
options.rationale: Spots below the surface dissolve into the pool instead of travelling up the paper, so nothing separates.

options.text: Otherwise the solvent front could not be marked at the end
options.rationale: A real step in the method is offered as the reason for an unrelated precaution.

mcqs.stem: A known dye X has an Rf value of 0.62 in a solvent. A mixture run in the same solvent gives spots at Rf 0.31, 0.62 and 0.85. What follows?

options.text: The mixture is dye X, since one spot has the same Rf value
options.rationale: A matching value is taken as proof of identity, and the other spots are ignored.

options.text: The mixture cannot contain X, because X gives only one spot
options.rationale: The one-spot test for a pure compound is misapplied to a mixture containing it.

options.text: The mixture contains X, and the other spots are the solvent
options.rationale: The extra spots are explained away as the solvent rather than as further compounds.

options.text: The mixture may contain X, along with two other compounds
options.rationale: A matching Rf value in the same solvent is information that helps identify a compound, and the other two spots are further compounds.

mcqs.stem: What can paper chromatography do for a mixture of coloured substances?

options.text: Separate it and give information helping to identify parts
options.rationale: This is what the specification claims for chromatography: separation, plus information that helps identification.

options.text: Name every substance in it without using any known samples
options.rationale: The chromatogram is thought to identify substances by itself, without reference runs.

options.text: Show how much of each substance the mixture contains
options.rationale: Spot size is read as a measure of the amount present.

options.text: Split each substance in it into the elements it contains
options.rationale: Chromatography is confused with a method that breaks compounds down.
